segments.title: Four books for studying naval history by period
segments.body: The four books are grouped by the periods they cover rather than by a single ship or battle. Together they offer a chronological route from the emergence of state navies through sail and steam to the Second World War. Wide-period surveys can help a reader connect organizational change, warship design, and operations across centuries.

evidence.note: Books designed to encompass particular historical periods.

segments.summary: The episode introduces four broad surveys whose date ranges provide entry points into naval institutions, warfare, technology, and operations from 1500 to 1945.

segments.title: How permanent state navies displaced older armed institutions
segments.body: Glete contrasts medieval armed society, including local levies, militias, armed merchants, private castles, and military entrepreneurs, with salaried organizations controlled by a central state. The book uses Max Weber's organizational theory to ask why permanent armies and navies ultimately proved superior to competing arrangements. Written command systems, professional careers, separation of public and private assets, and institutional archives all become part of the explanation. Samuel McLean's research through Global Maritime History offers a further route into the subject. The book links naval development directly to the formation of early-modern states.

evidence.note: The passage contrasts social, market, and permanent state systems for organizing warfare.
Organizational theory and state formation are presented as the book's central value.

segments.summary: Jan Glete's Warfare at Sea, 1500-1650 frames the rise of centralized navies as an organizational change from feudal, mercantile, and hired forces to permanent state institutions.

segments.title: The Dutch invasion of 1688 and an English fleet that did not fight
segments.body: William III assembled 11,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry aboard 250 merchantmen, protected by 39 battleships, 26 frigates, 10 fireships, and 20 other vessels, but planned to avoid the English fleet rather than defeat it. Arthur Herbert, an English naval officer who had joined William, commanded the invasion fleet with instructions to dissuade his former colleagues from attacking. The English expected a northern landing, while favorable easterly winds pinned Dartmouth's ships behind the Gunfleet Sands as the Dutch sailed west and landed at Torbay. French strategic misreading, exaggerated reports, changing winds, and uncertainty over loyalties further discouraged an interception. The invasion succeeded without the fleet action that raw force comparisons might suggest was necessary.

evidence.note: The Dutch invasion force, escorts, and plan to avoid battle are described.
French misreading, winds, the Torbay landing, and the English decision not to attack explain the bloodless naval outcome.

segments.summary: Richard Harding's Sea Power and Naval Warfare, 1650-1830 uses William III's invasion to show how weather, intelligence, political support, and caution neutralized a powerful English fleet.

segments.title: Why political will can disable sea power
segments.body: The English officers understood the limits of Dutch naval power, yet chose not to shape the land campaign after William's army came ashore. Harding's interpretation emphasizes caution, career interests, divided allegiance, and political confusion rather than a simple operational inability to fight. A large and professional navy was therefore immobilized by a small number of decisions. The apparent ease of the invasion also made defense against seaborne attack a stronger influence on later English naval development.

evidence.note: The passage asks why the fleet did not intervene and identifies the choice as political rather than military.
Political confusion disables the navy and the invasion reshapes perceptions of fleet defense.

segments.summary: The 1688 campaign shows that ships and professional skill do not create sea power without political cohesion and a willingness to employ the fleet.

segments.title: British turret ships from Prince Albert to Captain
segments.body: During the American Civil War, the Royal Navy kept unusually large squadrons at Halifax and Bermuda but sent no armored warships across the Atlantic, while British private yards laid down warships for the Confederacy and the royal dockyards continued building ironclads. News from Hampton Roads accelerated European debate between monitors and armored frigates, although Britain had already ordered the coastal turret ship Prince Albert. Prince Albert's four Cowper Coles turrets turned on rollers below deck, unlike John Ericsson's centrally pivoted turret, and each mounted a single 9-inch gun. The converted Royal Sovereign carried four turrets with heavier 10.5-inch ordnance, while the ocean-going Monarch mounted four 12-inch guns in two centreline turrets. HMS Captain then combined low freeboard, rig, and heavy turret armament in a design that capsized off Cape Finisterre in 1870. The sequence compares coastal and ocean-going solutions while showing the danger of forcing several competing requirements into one ship.

evidence.note: The passage covers Hampton Roads, Prince Albert, its turrets, and its long service.
Royal Sovereign, later turret ships, Monarch, and Captain's loss illustrate competing design solutions and risk.

segments.summary: Lawrence Sondhaus's Naval Warfare, 1815-1914 traces the Royal Navy's early turret ships and the design choices that culminated in HMS Captain's fatal stability problem.

segments.title: German heavy ships after the Norwegian campaign
segments.body: Scharnhorst remained at Trondheim for temporary repairs after HMS Acasta torpedoed her while defending HMS Glorious on 8 June 1940. When Scharnhorst and Gneisenau attempted to return to Germany, HMS Clyde torpedoed Gneisenau off Norway and forced her back into port while her sister reached Kiel. Both battlecruisers then underwent repairs, and Admiral Hipper's Arctic sortie was abortive. RAF attacks on Kiel and Wilhelmshaven did not seriously damage the ships, yet accumulated battle damage still produced a three-month lull in major German surface activity. Submarine and destroyer attacks, followed by repair time, shaped the availability of the German surface fleet even though its capital ships survived.

evidence.note: The passage traces Scharnhorst and Gneisenau from damage off Norway through their return to Germany for repairs.
Admiral Hipper's abortive sortie, the operational lull, and ineffective RAF attacks describe the state of the German surface fleet.

segments.summary: Roskill's account follows Scharnhorst, Gneisenau, and Admiral Hipper through torpedo damage, repair, and the lull in German heavy-ship operations after Norway.

segments.title: Disguised German merchant raiders in 1940
segments.body: Germany kept pressure on Allied shipping through armed merchant raiders such as Atlantis, Orion, Widder, Thor, Pinguin, Komet, and Kormoran. Equipped with modern guns, torpedo tubes, and often reconnaissance aircraft, they used elaborate disguises and remote rendezvous with supply ships to remain at sea. They targeted isolated merchantmen, sometimes simulated distress or attacked at night, and shifted cruising grounds and identities when an area became dangerous. Their ability to range across the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans made them difficult to locate, while only cruiser-strength warships were considered powerful enough to engage them. Komet's Soviet-assisted passage along Siberia's northern coast also exposes the diplomatic and logistical support that enabled German commerce raiding early in the war.

evidence.note: The passage names the disguised raiders, explains their tactics and support, and describes Komet's northern passage.

segments.summary: Roskill's The War at Sea, 1939-1945 explains how seven disguised merchant raiders attacked Allied shipping across distant ocean routes while most large German surface ships lay in home waters.
